item.description:
Philippe Decouflé’s staging of Haruki Murakami’s epic dual-narrative novel at the Barbican is ‘one long immaculate coup de théâtre’, writes Arifa Akbar.

End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to life

Barbican theatre, London
With a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicorns

9 October 2026

Arifa Akbar

Beautiful but dangerous … Kiita Komagine and Misato Morita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian

How to stage Haruki Murakami’s epic, dual-narrative novel without leaving the audience in a muddle? Director-choreographer Philippe Decouflé goes big, filling the enormous Barbican stage with a kaleidoscope of dream worlds for Ako Takahashi’s adaptation. It could have become a scramble of stories and inquiries into memory, technological advances in society and the imagination. Instead, it is turned into one long immaculate coup de théâtre.

There are two versions of the protagonist, Watashi (Tatsuya Fujiwara) – one is in Tokyo, the other in a world comprising dreams. The city is noirish while the latter is beautiful but dangerous, with a complicated storyline involving the sundering of humans from their shadows, a walled city, roaming animals and a professor (Narushi Ikeda) who collects their skulls to channel past experiences through sound.

Rabbit hole of wonderlands … Miu Tomita plays Woman in Pink and Tatsuya Fujiwara is Watashi. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian

The professor’s 17-year-old granddaughter (Miu Tomita) accompanies Watashi in Tokyo and appears like a kitsch version of the prophetess who goes with Aeneas into the underworld. Watashi seeks escape, so he can be reunited with his shadow (Shuntaro Miyao), but is drawn to this strange world too and has a romance with a librarian (Misato Morita).

Initially, it spirals into a rabbit hole of wonderlands, with kooky humour and references to western canonical and pop culture, as is Murakami’s way, from ancient myth to Lewis Carroll’s Alice and Luis Buñuel’s Un Chien Andalou. A playful set, designed by K Ishihara, shows its own theatrical construction with cheeky playfulness.

The visual pyrotechnics suck you in, from big projections to the speed, flow and agility of dancing that gestures at anime. They bring forth Murakami’s many creatures, from underground “murks”, with porcupine spikes, who flip and cartwheel, to a herd of balletic unicorns.

Decouflé’s choreography is unsurpassable in its elastic grace and athleticism without seeming circus-like. The aesthetics on the whole are so ravishing that it doesn’t matter if the story is not easy to grasp in the first half. At least not for some because, while Murakami fans will know that the unity of the story is to come, initiates to his work may be left punch-drunk and befuddled by the onslaught of worlds and images.

It becomes clear after the interval that this is controlled and deliberate confusion, reflecting Watashi’s state of mind. The dance becomes imbued with feeling as Murakami’s world reveals its underlying themes of loneliness, grief, the fear of disappearing and of death.

But the story of lost shadows, representing the “true” self, bears bigger socio-political echoes that feel contemporary, and even prescient (the book was published in 1985). This world looks like Neo’s in The Matrix, and its technology chimes with ideas in Naomi Klein’s book, Doppelganger: A Trip into the Mirror World. The sinister side of the perfectionism that this dream society has cultivated could be a comment on postwar Japan, or on our world of AI, real and fake selves, code and machine-constructed subjectivity.

At almost three hours, it leaves you with the sense that you have been dreaming, collectively, about a world of dead animals, lost shadows and unfeeling humans, but also of unicorns, impossible beauty and an ocean-like imagination. It is both of our world, and other.

At Barbican theatre, London until 11 October

item.title: Day 14 · 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize (BBC)
item.description:
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson, 76, has won this year's Nobel Prize in Literature. The Swedish Academy praised her 'bold and inventive oeuvre' in playful dialogue with the classical tradition.

‘Bold and inventive’ Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize

8 October 2026

Ian Youngs, Culture reporter

Alamy

Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year’s Nobel Prize in Literature.

Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.

The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.

Carson responded by joking that the judges were “crazy” for honouring her. “I think they’re all crazy… Well, you know, it’s crazy,” she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying.

The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime’s body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m).

Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement.

“She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind,” Carlberg, said.

“She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”

Getty Images: Anne Carson pictured in 1998

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson lives in Michigan and has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022.

Anders Olsson, chairman of the Swedish Academy’s Nobel committee for Literature, praised the way Carson has “broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature”.

“This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms,” he said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Carson’s win was “an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada”.

The writer’s works feature “wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own,” Carney wrote on social media.

“She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature.”

Carson’s notable works include The Glass Essay, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, Nox, Float and The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos.

In 2019, her performance piece Norma Jeane Baker of Troy drew a line between famous beauties from different historical periouds - Helen of Troy and Marilyn Monroe.

In 2021, she released The Trojan Women: A Comic, a graphic retelling of Euripides’ ancient story; and her translation of Elektra by Sophocles was staged starring Brie Larson in London last year.

She has been a professor of classics for more than 30 years and her writing is often inspired by Greek literature.

Her translations have often given a contemporary twist to ancient works.

“Her collaborations with visual artists and choreographers and with opera and theatre directors demonstrate the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems,” Olsson said.

“It is this that lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene.”

Thousands of Stuart Hall's papers, notebooks, recordings and videos go online in a new digital archive at the University of Birmingham, which bars AI bots from scraping the data.

Thatcherism via the Walkman: Stuart Hall’s British cultural studies preserved online

Project lead says it celebrates ‘incredible contributions’ Jamaica-born sociologist made to Britain’s culture

7 October 2026

Chris Osuh

Stuart Hall in 2007. He used the Sony Walkman as a case study of how social, cultural and economic life can be expressed through a single technology. Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Observer

Whether it was Thatcherism, populism or the story of the Sony Walkman, Stuart Hall was a public intellectual famed for defining the times. Now a major digital archive of his previously unpublished papers, notebooks, recordings and videos has been launched.

When the Jamaica-born sociologist and seminal figure in postwar Black British history died in 2014 aged 82, his obituary in the Guardian said he had been “among the first to identify key questions of the age”. Hall coined the term Thatcherism and in 1985 warned of the dangers of “authoritarian populism”.

The University of Birmingham, where Hall developed the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, has digitised and released more than 3,100 items donated by his widow, the historian Catherine Hall.

They include notebooks, index cards, his abandoned doctoral thesis and hours of previously inaccessible audio and video tracing the evolution of cultural studies, all within an interactive database.

Hall’s notes, charting the development of cultural studies, have been preserved in the archive. Photograph: University of Birmingham

Also released are his “Origins of the new left” lecture, notebooks on “race and moral panics”, and Encoding/Decoding Cybernetics, a research project exploring Hall’s impact on the architecture of large language models.

In response to the era of artificial intelligence, and the questions it raises about culture, copyright and corporate power, the academics behind the Stuart Hall Archive Project have barred AI bots from accessing the data.

The Cadbury Research Library, which has catalogued the original papers, has run the digital archive through a programme that “poisons the data” for bots.

The project lead, Dr Rebecca Roach, working with Helen Fisher and Dr Katherine Parson, said they did not create the archive “just for AI to scrape” and commercialise. She said the platform was built to ensure “it doesn’t replicate the exploitation of people of colour and their cultural heritage that technology has historically enabled”.

“One of the things that was really central to us developing the Stuart Hall digital site was to think about what can we learn from Hall’s ideas – and how can we apply that to our current moment with machine learning,” Roach said.

Hall died before the AI era fully arrived, but he left a body of work with which to interpret it. His theory of representation – examining how media builds meaning through language, symbols and cultural codes – remains relevant amid concerns about algorithmic bias. Doing Cultural Studies, a textbook he co-authored, used the Walkman as a case study of how social, cultural and economic life could be expressed through a single technology.

Roach said it was important to celebrate Black British intellectuals who had made “incredible contributions” to British culture, and noted that while scholars had sometimes been “a bit sniffy” about popular culture, Hall was at its forefront. She called him “a guiding figure for making the world better”.

Alongside the archive, Roach has produced learning materials for primary schoolchildren, while the art collective Vivid Projects has made a zine called Dear Stuart.

University of Birmingham students have created Walking with Hall, a virtual tour of campus landmarks, raising questions about what it meant for the academic to walk in the shadow of Joseph Chamberlain, the imperialist statesman who founded the university.

Classically educated in Jamaica, Hall came to Britain in 1951 on a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, became the founding editor of New Left Review, and worked as a supply teacher in Brixton before pursuing his academic career.

He met Catherine on an anti-nuclear march in 1963; they moved to Birmingham, where their two children were born and where he made his university department a beacon for debate on media, race, politics, Marxism and critical theory.

From 1997 to 2000 he served on the Runnymede Trust’s commission on the future of multi-ethnic Britain, going on to collaborate with young artists and film-makers, and in 2005 he was made a fellow of the British Academy.

Calling the archive “an extraordinary resource”, Prof Daniel McNeil, the Stuart Hall interdisciplinary chair at Birmingham University, said Hall “transformed how we think about culture, identity, power and belonging”.

item.description:
Prof Francis Halzen wins the Nobel Prize in Physics for leading the IceCube observatory at the South Pole, built to detect 'ghost particles' called neutrinos from distant galaxies.

‘Ghost particles’ from space telescope wins physics Nobel

6 October 2026

Pallab Ghosh, Science correspondent

Yuya Makino/IceCube/NSF: Prof Francis Halzen won for “decisive contribution” to developing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory

Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe.

Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said “his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory”.

He first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988.

Halzen, who is now a US citizen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, told a news conference that he was surprised his idea worked so well.

“I have to emphasise how lucky I was. Because when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself.”

Neutrinos are elusive subatomic particles. The Sun produces vast numbers of them: every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail.

But IceCube is searching for much higher-energy neutrinos, those produced by violent processes far beyond our Solar System — in distant galaxies.

It is composed of thousands of sensors on long cables that are drilled and frozen into a 1km cubic block of ice.

Neutrinos can be thought of as astronomical messengers that point to those fundamental events.

At the observatory, most neutrinos pass straight through the ice, but occasionally one interacts with it, producing particles that give off a telltale flash of light.

These rare signals carry clues to where the neutrinos came from and the extreme conditions that produced them — allowing scientists to investigate places that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see.

“Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument,” said Prof Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.

“His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.”

IceCube/NSF: This blurry image is of the Milky Way, but it is composed of neutrino particles

On the rare occasions when a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it produces fast-moving charged particles. It is these racing through the ice, which give off a blue glow, which sensitive light detectors can pick up.

The pattern and timing of that light allow scientists to estimate the direction the neutrino came from — helping them trace its origins in the cosmos. But these interactions are so rare that the observatory needed an enormous volume of clear ice.

Halzen’s idea was to use a vast natural ice sheet in Antarctica. So began an audacious plan to build a neutrino observatory at the geographic South Pole, with thousands of light sensors embedded deep in the ice.

The neutrino’s ghostly nature, the very thing that makes it so hard to detect, also makes it a powerful messenger from the distant Universe.

Neutrinos rarely interact with material in its way, so they can go right through dense regions that light cannot easily penetrate.

And because they have no electric charge, magnetic fields do not bend their paths through space. That means their direction of arrival can point scientists back towards their source.

Their energies carry further insight into the processes that created them - helping scientists investigate how exploding stars and the environments around giant black holes accelerate particles to extraordinary energies.

Louis Barson, director of science at the Institute of Physics in London, said the IceCube Observatory had enabled astronomers to investigate phenomena that conventional telescopes cannot see.

“The discoveries that have followed are helping us understand some of the most energetic and mysterious processes in the universe - and that’s thanks to Professor Halzen’s work,” he added.

Prof Subir Sarkar, physicist from the University of Oxford, quoted the French novelist Marcel Proust in describing his assessment of Halzen’s contribution to science:

“‘The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is’.

“Francis Halzen has led the IceCube collaboration on just such a voyage of discovery and opened a new window on to our Universe”.

Prof Francis Halzen wins the Nobel Prize in Physics for leading the IceCube observatory at the South Pole, built to detect 'ghost particles' called neutrinos from distant galaxies.

‘Ghost particles’ from space telescope wins physics Nobel

6 October 2026

Pallab Ghosh, Science correspondent

Yuya Makino/IceCube/NSF: Prof Francis Halzen won for “decisive contribution” to developing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory

Belgian-born physicist Prof Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on an observatory that detects particles from space, shedding light on the distant universe.

Halzen led the development of IceCube at the South Pole, which uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice fitted with light sensors to detect particles called neutrinos. These carry information about violent, high-energy processes in the cosmos.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said “his vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory”.

He first presented his vision for detecting neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988.

Halzen, who is now a US citizen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, told a news conference that he was surprised his idea worked so well.

“I have to emphasise how lucky I was. Because when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself.”

Neutrinos are elusive subatomic particles. The Sun produces vast numbers of them: every second, billions pass harmlessly through an area the size of your fingernail.

But IceCube is searching for much higher-energy neutrinos, those produced by violent processes far beyond our Solar System — in distant galaxies.

It is composed of thousands of sensors on long cables that are drilled and frozen into a 1km cubic block of ice.

Neutrinos can be thought of as astronomical messengers that point to those fundamental events.

At the observatory, most neutrinos pass straight through the ice, but occasionally one interacts with it, producing particles that give off a telltale flash of light.

These rare signals carry clues to where the neutrinos came from and the extreme conditions that produced them — allowing scientists to investigate places that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see.

“Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument,” said Prof Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.

“His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.”

IceCube/NSF: This blurry image is of the Milky Way, but it is composed of neutrino particles

On the rare occasions when a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it produces fast-moving charged particles. It is these racing through the ice, which give off a blue glow, which sensitive light detectors can pick up.

The pattern and timing of that light allow scientists to estimate the direction the neutrino came from — helping them trace its origins in the cosmos. But these interactions are so rare that the observatory needed an enormous volume of clear ice.

Halzen’s idea was to use a vast natural ice sheet in Antarctica. So began an audacious plan to build a neutrino observatory at the geographic South Pole, with thousands of light sensors embedded deep in the ice.

The neutrino’s ghostly nature, the very thing that makes it so hard to detect, also makes it a powerful messenger from the distant Universe.

Neutrinos rarely interact with material in its way, so they can go right through dense regions that light cannot easily penetrate.

And because they have no electric charge, magnetic fields do not bend their paths through space. That means their direction of arrival can point scientists back towards their source.

Their energies carry further insight into the processes that created them - helping scientists investigate how exploding stars and the environments around giant black holes accelerate particles to extraordinary energies.

Louis Barson, director of science at the Institute of Physics in London, said the IceCube Observatory had enabled astronomers to investigate phenomena that conventional telescopes cannot see.

“The discoveries that have followed are helping us understand some of the most energetic and mysterious processes in the universe - and that’s thanks to Professor Halzen’s work,” he added.

Prof Subir Sarkar, physicist from the University of Oxford, quoted the French novelist Marcel Proust in describing his assessment of Halzen’s contribution to science:

“‘The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is’.

“Francis Halzen has led the IceCube collaboration on just such a voyage of discovery and opened a new window on to our Universe”.

item.title: Day 11 · Children’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study shows (Guardian)
item.description:
New research into UK publishing shows children’s books with Black main characters fell by almost 8% last year, while disabled representation in picture books dropped sharply too.

Children’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study shows

Only 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent characters

5 October 2026

Emma Loffhagen

Just 47 of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character, Photograph: MBI/Alamy

The number of children’s books featuring Black main characters fell by almost 8% last year, according to research into diversity in UK publishing.

Just 47 – or 2.1% – of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character, a 7.8% fall from the previous year, according to Inclusive Books for Children. Black children make up about 8.5% of that age bracket in England and Wales.

Representation of south Asian main characters fell by 14.3 percentage points to 1.4%, despite children of south Asian heritage making up about 12.4% of the population of under-10s. Just three books featured main characters of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) heritage, down 50% from the previous year. This represented 0.1% of surveyed books, compared with the group’s 2.2% share of the population.

The research by the literacy charity found that only 150 books – 6.9% of those surveyed – featured main characters from minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent backgrounds. Of these, 37.3% were written or illustrated by creators who did not share the background of their characters.

The author Serena Patel said: “At an age when children are figuring out the world around them and where they fit in, it’s vital they have access to funny, inspiring, adventurous books that reflect both the lives they live and the ones they don’t. We must do better.”

The report surveyed baby and toddler books, picture books and fiction for children aged up to nine. It found that representation of disabled characters in picture books fell sharply: the number with disabled main characters dropped by 60% in 2025, to just two titles. Neither was by a disabled creator.

The survey also highlighted what it described as a lack of “incidental representation”: stories in which a main character’s identity does not explicitly drive the plot of the story.

Dr Stella Louis, an early years consultant, trainer and author, pointed to this “continued reliance” on books where identity itself was the story. “Why can’t a child simply be south Asian, disabled, neurodivergent or bilingual and also be the hero of an ordinary story about friendship, adventure, loss or joy?” she said.

The report found that all three books published in 2025 with MENA main characters were refugee narratives. The study authors said children of MENA heritage needed stories covering a broader range of themes and experiences.

“As an Arab author, it is painful to see the number of children’s fiction books representing our region decline from six to only three in 2025,” said Nadine Kaadan. She said the fact that all three books published were focused on refugee experiences risked reinforcing a “single story” about the region, defining it through “war and displacement rather than our rich cultures and heritage”.

There were some signs of progress. Neurodivergent representation increased in picture books, from three titles in 2024 to 13 last year. In the baby and toddler category, the number of books with marginalised main characters rose by 29.4%.

Jake Hope, a children’s book consultant, said: “When children’s enjoyment of reading is at a significant low, it’s more important than ever that the stories children encounter reflect their lives, identities, experiences and emotions.

“These figures need to be more than mere statistics and a call to action for continued change and improvements.”

This article was amended on 5 October 2026. In an earlier version Serena Patel was misidentified as Sheena Patel. This has been corrected, and an image of Sheena Patel removed. The first name of Jake Hope was also corrected.

item.title: Day 10 · Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies (BBC)
item.description:
New data shows Swiss glaciers lost more than 5% of their remaining ice in the past 12 months. Scientists warn the rapid melting could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.

Swiss glaciers suffer ‘disastrous’ year of ice loss, threatening water supplies

1 October 2026

Mark Poynting, Climate reporter

L.Hösli: The front of Morteratsch Glacier in south-east Switzerland, which has been attacked by warm air and water

Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.

More than 5% of the country’s remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is “extraordinary”.

They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.

The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.

There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.

But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.

Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be “extreme”. This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.

“It’s really just disastrous,” said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.

Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.

And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below.

Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun’s energy.

That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.

“Ten years ago, I wouldn’t have thought that it’s possible to lose glaciers so quickly,” said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.

“What’s happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist’s perspective,” he added.

Five images of Rhône Glacier, in each year from 2022 to 2026. The glacier flows from top to bottom of the image, with steep valley walls on either side. The glacier has noticeably retreated and thinned over this period. A lake covers where ice used to be.

Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.

Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.

Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.

The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.

“Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that’s been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago,” said Huss.

“It’s helping us [now] but it’s unsustainable, so we won’t have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave.”

The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer, affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.

One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.

Community-funded excavations on the Scottish island of Lismore have uncovered a sixth-century monastery with rare traces of gold- and silver-working, rewriting the island’s story.

‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity

Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore

1 October 2026

Esther Addley

Islanders and volunteers have been digging in the early medieval cemetery, where they have discovered the earlier buildings, burial grounds and other finds. Photograph: Robert Hay

To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island.

This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history.

A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west.

In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say.

To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland – it’s extraordinary,” he said.

A crucible freshly out of the soil. Photograph: Robert Hay

“The most exciting moment for me was when they were doing the post-excavation analysis and they found that they had been melting gold, copper, silver, and they were making jewellery on our little island in the seventh century.”

While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. Raising the low five-figure sum needed to pay for it all had been “just a business of getting down to it and organising and so on”, he said. “It was actually a lot easier than what my previous job used to be.”

Gordon Noble, a professor of archaeology at the University of Aberdeen, said the finds were highly significant. “We know about sites like Iona having these very famous monastic sites from this early medieval world. But apart from the association with Moluag and a piece of sculpture from this site, we knew practically nothing really about Lismore. So it was hugely exciting to see the results emerging through the local group’s work with Clare [Ellis] … This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment.”

While professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.”

Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.”

The results of the community excavations will be published in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity.

item.title: Day 8 · Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently (BBC)
item.description:
Greek PM Kyriakos Mitsotakis urges Andy Burnham to find the political will to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece for good, rejecting the British Museum's suggestion that the Bayeux Tapestry loan offers a template for a deal. (BBC News, 24 September 2026.)

Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently

24 September 2026

Katie Razzall, Culture and media editor

In Pictures via Getty Images: Some of the Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum. The sculptures are damaged, with some missing limbs and heads

The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the “political will” to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would “send a powerful signal” but would require “courage”.

The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.

The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country’s claim to the Elgin Marbles.

“Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it,” he wrote on Thursday.

“Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures.”

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was “surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures”, adding: “I do not believe it does.”

“Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we ‘borrow’ parts of our own monument,” he wrote.

Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.

This would be a “decisive step”, Mitsotakis said, that would “reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship”.

Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with “no strings attached”.

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that “ultimately it’s an issue for the British Museum”, adding that “legally that’s where that issue rests”.

Bloomberg via Getty Images: Many of the Elgin Marbles originate from the Parthenon in Athens

British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.

They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.

After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin’s actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.

The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.

The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.

Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a “more co-operative arrangement” after “quite a bitter disagreement” with the Greeks for more than 200 years.

Mitsotakis’s latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.

Last month, Greece’s health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.

The British Museum’s position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.

Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

item.title: Day 7 · Oxford lets OpenAI train its AI models on Bodleian Library (Guardian)
item.description:
Internal documents show the University of Oxford has let OpenAI train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, while staff minutes record concerns over reputational risk. (The Guardian, 26 September 2026.)

Oxford lets OpenAI train its AI models on Bodleian Library

University staff voice concerns over reputational risk of partnering with company behind ChatGPT

26 September 2026

Ethan Penny and Dan Milmo

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, has been digitising material from Oxford’s Bodleian Library to populate its training set. Photograph: Michael Dwyer/AP

The University of Oxford has allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data.

The Bodleian material digitised by OpenAI has been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents.

Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers.

However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data.

An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was “proud” to ensure “the AI models of today preserve the world’s historical knowledge for the future”.

“With more than a billion people using this technology in everyday life, it’s important it reflects different cultures, histories and perspectives,” they added.

Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology.

Booksellers have also reported a spate of orders for obscure titles such as a guide to agricultural implements in 18th-century Africa or biographies of 1950s car drivers. Secondhand bookshop owners have speculated that because the titles are unlikely to exist online in digitised form, they represent fresh data that can be consumed by the next generation of AI models.

Scraped websites are increasingly saturated with AI-generated material, making them less useful for training models, and developers have turned to physical, often historical, book collections.

OpenAI has struck similar agreements with US research libraries such as Boston Public Library, Caltech, MIT, and the University of Michigan under a project called NextGenAI. Oxford is the only UK member of the project.

By June 2025, 125,000 images scanned from historical dissertations had been shared with OpenAI from the Bodleian collection, including PhD theses from European and American universities written in the 19th and 20th centuries. Other texts scanned include a rare collection of 10,000 16th-century “broadside ballads” containing song lyrics and musical notes that were once circulated on Tudor street corners. Staff have also discussed digitising of 18th-century Irish state papers, the private letters of Irish novelist Marie Edgeworth, and Dorothy Hodgkin’s penicillin notebooks.

The OpenAI contract with Oxford also raises the prospect of the mass digitisation of the Bodleian’s collection consisting of 23m items. The minutes also discussed the creation of an “Ask the Bod” chatbot.

A spokesperson for the University of Oxford said the amount of text being digitised was “modest in scale” and covered only out-of-copyright material. The Bodleian keeps the rights to the scans and will begin publishing them openly online within months, the spokesperson said.

They rejected the suggestion that the machine-learning element had been hidden from the public and students. Digitisation was the university’s primary interest, said the spokesperson, but staff had been open that the project would also contribute training data.

The Bodleian’s collections remain intact under the deal, unlike with secondhand book acquisitions elsewhere that are being pulped after scanning. Anthropic, OpenAI’s close rival, has spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring books and slicing off their spines so their contents can be scanned before having them pulped. Anthropic has said it does not buy and destroy rare and antiquarian books.

A tech news site, 404 Media, also placed a tracking device inside a secondhand book order and traced it to an Amazon facility in the US, where the books were also dismantled and scanned.

The Oxford spokesperson said: “The material digitised through the project with OpenAI is modest in scale, out of copyright, and OpenAI’s use of the material is not exclusive.

“The Bodleian libraries also retain the rights to make the digitised material available themselves, and the library will begin to publish these materials openly online in the next few months, as we do with outputs from other digitisation partnerships.

“The project will in fact allow the Bodleian to make the material more accessible to a wider number for people, who might otherwise have found it difficult to access.”

Library’s first edition reveals Austen’s early fans

26 September 2026

Bea Swallow, West of England

Longleat House: The book is evidence Austen’s novels were being read and collected by the country-house elite during her own lifetime, say historians

A first edition of Jane Austen’s debut novel has shed light on the author’s connection with one of Britain’s historic country houses.

The 1811 first edition of Sense and Sensibility is on the shelves at Longleat House in Wiltshire, with its title page still carrying the anonymous attribution “By A Lady”.

It is thought to have been acquired by the 2nd Marquess of Bath around the time of its publication which historians say is evidence Austen was being read by the elite social class during her lifetime.

Dr James Ford, curator of Longleat House, said the estate had “a wonderful group of early Jane Austen editions”, including Emma and Pride and Prejudice.

Sense and Sensibility follows the Dashwood sisters after their father’s death leaves the family facing financial uncertainty. It follows the very different ways two young women navigate love, loss and society.

Bound in green and brown leather with a gold title, the relatively unassuming volume is among thousands of books in the seven historic libraries at Longleat House.

It is presumed Jane Austen signed her first novel “By a Lady” to maintain her anonymity.

Writing novels for money or public fame was generally considered unfeminine and improper for women of the gentry class during the 18th and 19th centuries.

Her identity as the author only became widely known after Austen’s death in 1817, when her brother Henry identified his sister in a biographical notice.

The libraries at Longleat House contain a total collection of around 44,000 historic books, including first editions of Emma and a second edition of Pride and Prejudice.

Getty/Andrew_Harker: Longleat House has seven libraries containing a total collection of about 44,000 historic books

“He was also one of the first owners of Longleat to open his park gates and hall door to early tourists, rather like the country house visit Austen evokes when Elizabeth Bennet arrives at Pemberley in Pride and Prejudice.”

The historic libraries and rare book collections at Longleat can be visited as part of its Libraries VIP Tour.

France's most prestigious literary prize withdraws a Canadian-Haitian writer's novel from its longlist after an anonymous X account alleged it was 'almost entirely' written by AI — the author denies the claim and calls it racially motivated. (The Guardian, 25 September 2026.)

Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list

Thélyson Orélien had been in the running to win a top literary prize before the AI claim emerged on social media

25 September 2026

Philip Oltermann, European culture editor

The author Thélyson Orélien, whose book, C’était ça ou mourir, has sold about 35,000 copies. Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images

The organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had removed a critically acclaimed novel by a Canadian-Haitian writer from the longlist after an anonymous online account claimed the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, said on Friday its decision to withdraw Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die) was “driven by the desire to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt prize and the academy itself, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men”.

The Haiti-born author’s book is a lyrical first-person account of how a history and geography teacher flees a home country mired in gang violence and embarks on a perilous journey across 12 countries before finding a haven in Canada.

Published in France by Grasset in August, it has sold about 35,000 copies and won the Prix du roman Fnac, with translation rights sold to more than 20 countries.

The novel on display inside a bookstore in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

Allegations that the book was written using AI emerged on X on 21 September, the same day It Was That or Die won the Fnac prize for best novel.

An anonymous account called Balance ton Claude – a reference to Anthropic’s AI agent – said it had fed the novel into the AI detection software Pangram and found it to be “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.

Questions have been raised over Pangram’s accuracy, and French media outlets have found other AI detection programmes that identified It Was That or Die as very probably written by a human.

Orélien, 38, has denied the allegation, saying it was racially motivated. “I’ve always loved creating and writing,” he said. “I don’t see why I would use a machine.”

He told the newspaper Libération that he used traditional language and rhythms that were Haitian and Caribbean. “The imagery, repetition and rhythm are a living language, they are mine.”

The author of the anonymous X account was later identified on the pages of the centre-right newspaper Le Figaro as one of its own columnists, Samuel Fitoussi, the author of an essay against “wokeism” on film and TV.

On his own X account, Fitoussi said he had initiated his campaign because even though he was “techno-optimistic”, he feared that “AI will cause the disappearance of reading and writing”.

On Wednesday Philippe Claudel, the Académie Goncourt’s president, had urged caution over the allegations. But separate accusations of plagiarism against Orélien published in French media appeared to have caused a change of heart.

Libération alleged in an article that the author plagiarised an award-winning short story from the preface of the French journalist Louis Pauwels’ book The Morning of the Magicians, originally published in 1960.

In its statement the academy referred to the “plagiarisms of which its author has been guilty over time and which have just been revealed, as well as the convergent result of several analyses by trustworthy researchers and journalists highlighting the fact that [the book] is in all likelihood very largely the product of artificial intelligence”.

“The aim is to send a clear message,” it added, “to affirm that we neither endorse nor condone in any way the creation of texts generated with the help of AI.”

In a statement shared with the Guardian, the novel’s original publisher, Le Éditions du Boréal, said: “Unfortunately, at this stage, we are unable to confirm or deny the allegations the author is facing.”

The Canada-based publisher said it was important not tojump to conclusions, adding: “Without credible, concrete evidence, it is not our place to decide whether this book has a right to exist.”

Boréal said it was “concerned” about the newer plagiarism allegations, but added it was important to remember there was a real person behind the book. “We unequivocally condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days, and we urge everyone to show restraint,” it said.

Orélien has said he will not comment further on the latest allegations. Speaking on Thursday at Les Correspondances literary festival in Manosque, southern France, he said: “There’s this desire not only to attack the book, but especially my voice … to silence me,” adding that he would therefore “take a step back and wait until things have calmed down”.

The Académie Goncourt will publish its shortlist on 6 October and announce the winner of the prize on 4 November.

Ruth Padel reviews Kate Mosse's new book Autumn — a love-song to West Sussex and a meditation on the turning of the seasons. (The Guardian, 22 September 2026.)

Autumn by Kate Mosse review – tender reflections on time and place

The author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved Sussex

22 September 2026

Ruth Padel

A tunnel through trees near Chichester, West Sussex. Photograph: Patricia Hamilton/Getty Images

Kate Mosse’s new book is a love-song to West Sussex, part of a series designed to bring out its authors’ personal connections to a home landscape. It began last year, with Michael Morpurgo welcoming spring in Devon, where he has lived – at the farm that inspired War Horse – for over 50 years; and then Val McDermid celebrating winter in Scotland, where she grew up and still lives. Bernardine Evaristo will explore summer soon – but, meanwhile, we have Mosse, also deeply and endearingly rooted in her chosen patch.

Mosse grew up in the village of Fishbourne. She now lives in Chichester, where she got to know her husband when they revised for A-levels in the shadow of the Bishop’s Palace, and held hands when she turned 17 on the day of the city’s annual Sloe Fair. Twenty-three years later, they celebrated her 40th there, with their children. Today, they live with his 90-something mother Granny Rosie – also “Sussex to her bones” – who remembers watching cattle herded in fields where a supermarket now stands.

In Granny Rosie’s youth, “the link between tradition and the natural world was present in every part of everyday life”, and that connection is the real focus of Mosse’s book. She has spent nearly all of her 65 years in Sussex. Her Languedoc trilogy was inspired by her time in the Aude city of Carcassonne, but it was Sussex that gave her a taste for the combination of landscape, history and storytelling that drives her books. The county’s folklore and countryside informed her gothic thriller The Taxidermist’s Daughter, and it was the backdrop for her memoir about family care-giving, An Extra Pair of Hands.

Autumn gives us more of it. Walking under oak trees, Mosse pictures far off days when oaks were the only road signs. In her garden, she tells us that the Romans called wild cyclamen “earth truffle”, “believing that ill spells were ineffective where they were found”. If there is, at times, a touch of the guide-book in her telling, she wins your heart by the sheer joy she takes in the details.

Mosse sets out what Sussex gave other writers, too. William Blake drafted Jerusalem in Felpham, then threw a drunk soldier out of his garden and was tried in Chichester for sedition (all because the soldier claimed he insulted the king). He was acquitted, but “never set foot in Sussex again”. John Keats was inspired by Chichester’s architecture to write The Eve of St Agnes; Hilaire Belloc became Sussex’s unofficial poet laureate; and James Joyce lived in Bognor Regis while writing Finnegans Wake.

Above all, there is “the great Sussex writer”, Rudyard Kipling. I love imagining how that phrase will be read in India; but, in fact, Kipling wrote Kim while living in Sussex (where he moved to in the late 1800s). Just So Stories came immediately after, and in 1906 he made the village of Burwash the setting for Puck of Pook’s Hill.

In the manner of Kipling, Mosse takes infectious delight in weaving her memories through bronze age camps, iron age forts, wetlands, the downs and the Devil’s Dyke, composing a hymn to Sussex’s countryside and braiding rambly byways of fact and legend with personal memories.

She loves the place so much that you feel she would have written as joyfully about it at any time of year. But she takes autumn seriously as a season of transition, beginning with her first day at school. There she is, 60 years ago, on 1 September: “Four, rising five.” Her mother is waving goodbye and her world is about to expand. Then, she takes us through the ghosts of Halloween, Bonfire Night in Lewes and Harvest festival.

By the time she gets to the last day of November, Autumn itself feels like a kind of harvest. Mosse sees it as a thank you for “the gift of home”. For the luxury of enjoying, intensely, the land where grandparents, children and grandchildren still gather; and for sun-dappled village Englishness. “I take a deep breath to try and capture my pleasure at simply being here.”

item.description:
The pioneering novelist and theatre critic, first black president of the Edinburgh International Festival, has died.

British-American author and critic Bonnie Greer dies aged 77

16 September 2026

Paul Glynn, Culture reporter

Getty Images: Greer’s work often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions

British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with “profound sadness”, Greer’s widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made “an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life” with her “intelligence, courage and distinctive voice”.

He added: “To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her.”

Hutchins continued: “Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together.”

‘Courage, humour and humanity’

BBC presenter Clive Myrie led the tributes from elsewhere, posting on X: “This is such a shock. She was a friend and mentor and I will miss her with all my heart.”

Former deputy prime minister David Lammy called Greer “a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting”.

He added that she was “a true life force” and he would “never forget her quiet fearlessness taking on Nick Griffin” during an appearance with the then-British National Party (BNP) leader on the BBC’s Question Time in 2009.

Lammy added: “I will miss her mentorship, and her friendship.”

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Greer’s voice brought “courage, humour and humanity to Britain’s cultural conversation”.

He said: “She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too - I will miss her friendship enormously.”

Plays, novels and panel shows

Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan.

Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a frequent panellist on programmes like Question Time and Newsnight Review, debating the topics of the day.

She penned award-winning works like Munda Negra, which won her the Verity Bargate Award for best play, and novels such as Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009).

Once named by the Observer as one of the country’s leading public intellectuals, Greer’s work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled issues around culture, race and public institutions.

Getty Images: Greer was made an OBE for services to the arts in 2010

Speaking to the Guardian in 2016 in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement, Greer said: “When I wake up in the morning, I’m just myself. It’s only when I leave the door that I become a black woman to the world.”

She added: “I tell black women all the time, ‘Don’t apologise for yourself and keep your hair nappy. Make sure you are heard’.”

Greer served on the boards of cultural institutions including the British Museum, Royal Opera House and London Film School, and was chancellor of London’s Kingston University.

Her other published works include a memoir titled A Parallel Life and a biography of US poet and playwright Langston Hughes.

Also in 2009, her part-memoir, part-music-history book, Obama Music, was published.

Greer was made an OBE in 2010 for services to the arts.

In 2022, she was appointed as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.

Broadcaster and author John Simpson added to the tributes on Wednesday, posting: “So sad to hear of the death of the writer and critic Bonnie Greer.

“She was a good friend, and gave me strong support at a time I needed it. Fiercely intelligent, but always avoided personal attacks. A huge loss.”

Fellow journalist and broadcaster Sangita Myska, who interviewed Greer several times, recalled her as having been a “smart, sassy, firebrand who will be missed from our public discourse”.

The Oxford classicist who made Homer plain-English starts again from scratch.

Emily Wilson to retranslate the Odyssey from scratch

Writer who criticised Christopher Nolan film based on her 2017 translation is working on new version of Homer’s poem

1 September 2026

Emma Loffhagen

Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP

Emily Wilson, the first woman to translate Homer’s Odyssey into English, is to retranslate the ancient Greek epic poem from scratch less than a decade after the publication of her acclaimed version.

The announcement comes after Wilson attracted controversy this summer with a scathing assessment of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of the Odyssey, which she slammed for its “abysmal” writing and lack of sex scenes.

Wilson’s 2017 translation became a bestseller and was praised for making the 3,000-year-old epic poem modern and accessible.

“I’m now retranslating the Odyssey from scratch, with an approach closer to that of my translation of the Iliad, using somewhat more lines than the original, enabling more varied word-length and pacing,” she told the New York Times.

“It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version,” she told the AP. “I’m about halfway through.”

Nolan cited Wilson’s 2017 translation, including its opening sentence, “Tell me about a complicated man”, as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, released in July this year and starring Tom Holland, Zendaya, Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway.

Nolan’s adaptation took the global box office by storm, making $264m (£196m) during its opening weekend, marking the director’s best ever opening. Book sales saw a huge bump too: UK print sales of the poem increased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period in 2025, after the film’s release in the middle of the month.

Wilson made headlines for her attack on Nolan’s version. Writing in the London Review of Books, she said: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great … The writing is abysmal.”

She continued: “None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible,” adding, “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”

Her criticism attracted strong reactions, including from novelist Joyce Carol Oates, who accused Wilson of “haughty superiority”.

Wilson’s decision to retranslate the poem predates the row over the film. In an interview recorded in the spring for the ancient-history podcast Instant Classics, she discussed her desire to return to Homer and approach the poem differently from her first translation.

“I’m proud of my Odyssey translation … I think there are lots of good things about the kinds of compression and choices that I was forced into,” Wilson said then.

She has indicated that she will “probably” keep the opening line, “Tell me about a complicated man”. Wilson also added that her original translation relied too heavily on the word “slave”, when more precise terminology could have better reflected the different forms of enslavement depicted in the poem.

The new translation will also give readers far more of Wilson’s scholarly commentary. “I’m also going to quadruple the number of endnotes because endnotes are really fun to write,” she said.

While Wilson’s decision to retranslate Homer’s poem is unusual, it is not without precedent.

“Translators quite often rework or rewrite their own previous translations,” said Matthew Reynolds, professor of English and comparative criticism at Oxford University.

“Elizabeth Barrett Browning completely rewrote her translation of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound, Ezra Pound repeatedly revised his translations of Guido Cavalcanti, and Yu JongHo (유종호) translated Jane Eyre into Korean first in 1970 and again in 2004.”

He added: “It shows that translation – especially literary translation – is not just a matter of right or wrong, good or bad, but a continual exploratory process of interpretive reimagining and re-making.”

Wilson’s new Odyssey does not yet have a publication date.

item.description:
2000-year-old Roman wreck with amphorae hoard found near Mazara del Vallo.

Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast

9 August 2026

Ian Aikman and Mimi Swaby, global affairs reporters

Shipwreck with amphorae hoard discovered off Sicily coast

Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.

The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil.

Italy’s Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as “one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years”.

Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media.

The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC.

Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo.

He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner.

“I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn’t a rock,” he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae — tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain.

“This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life,” he said. “It’s hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again.”

Carabinieri via AFP: A diver in full scuba gear on the edge of a small boat in the sea

He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and “countless marine life” living among the jars, noting: “The sea never ceases to amaze us. This time we didn’t just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history.”

Specialist divers from the cultural heritage protection arm of Italy’s police, known as the Carabinieri Art Squad, were sent to the site.

Officials say safety measures will be taken to safeguard it while it undergoes investigation, as experts work to determine the nature of the wreck and learn more about its cargo.

The Mediterranean seabed is thought to be scattered with similar ancient wrecks. Another 1st or 2nd Century BC vessel was found north-west of Rome in 2023, again laden with hundreds of amphorae.

In 2018, a Greek merchant ship dating back more than 2,400 years was found lying on its side off the Bulgarian coast. At the time, it was hailed as the world’s oldest-known intact shipwreck.
